note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — EYEBROWS, THEN BRANCH TIP
tiles.details: Trace an undamaged mature comb to its far tip: blue grama's rachis ends in one or more rudimentary spikelets, NOT a conspicuous 5–20 mm naked sharp projection as in hairy grama. Count combs on one connected stem, not several overlapping stems. Existing photos show curved combs but do not prove a calibrated tip character.
tiles.short: Count 1–3(4) curved, one-sided combs on ONE flowering culm, each about 1.5–5 cm.
tiles.status: REAL COMB SILHOUETTE — MEASURED ATTACHED TIP STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · PERENNIAL CROWN AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Follow basal shoots to a single root crown. Short stout rhizomes can occur, but a low matlike stand photograph is NOT evidence of connected rhizomes or rooting stolons. Open the INNER blade–sheath junction to find the actual short ligule ring/fringe of hairs; separate it from longer lateral collar hairs. SDSU gives <0.5 mm; Utah flora describes the entire ring <1 mm. No archived image resolves the calibrated inner ligule.
tiles.short: Short-rhizomatous or densely tufted perennial; true ligule is a hair fringe generally <0.5–1 mm.

tiles.heading: 03 · COMB AND SPIKELET MEASUREMENTS
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase gives 1–3(4) arcuate branches 1.5–5 cm long and 5–6 mm laterally compressed spikelets. Count crowded spikelets along one intact branch; the literature often reports roughly 30–90 per branch, but no archived overview permits a precise count. Pale dangling anthers are NOT glumes, lemmas or awns. Photograph an attached mature comb beside a ruler.
tiles.short: Crowded one-sided combs ~1.5–5 cm; mature spikelet bodies usually ~5–6 mm, excluding awns.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — EXISTING IMAGES NOT CALIBRATED

tiles.heading: 04 · TWO GLUMES, FERTILE LEMMA AND ITS AWNS
tiles.details: Separate the persistent one-veined LOWER and UPPER glumes before measuring. Kew's GrassBase lower glume is narrower (~3–3.5 mm), while Go Botany includes ~1.5–3.5 mm; Kew upper glume ~5–6 mm and Go Botany ~3.5–6 mm. The basal fertile lemma is three-veined, ~4–6 mm in GrassBase, with central awn ~1–3 mm and shorter lateral awns ~0.5–2 mm. These are literature ranges, not measured from photos. Never assign a floret's awn to the branch rachis.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~1.5–3.5 mm; upper ~3.5–6 mm; fertile lemma ~4–6 mm with 3 short awns.

tiles.heading: 05 · STERILE FLORET AND CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: GrassBase describes a reduced apical sterile floret with three awns ~2–3 mm; a Utah flora treatment describes sterile awns ~2.5–5 mm. Dissect the reduced floret separately from the fertile lemma before placing awn arrows. Hairy grama (B. hirsuta) often has spreading hairs and a bare distal rachis; B. pectinata is generally taller with longer/more combs, but overlaps; Texas grama (B. rigidiseta) has several very short bristly units; sideoats grama (B. curtipendula) bears many branches down an extended axis. Reddish/purple color is not decisive.
tiles.short: Above the fertile floret, find 1(–2) reduced sterile florets; contrast hairy grama's naked branch-tip stinger.
tiles.status: REAL DIFFERENT-SPECIES COMPARISON — MATCHED SCALE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / TWO HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): source-authenticated Central Texas connected rooted crown with flowering culm and 1–3(4) combs; exposed 0.5–1 mm hair-fringe ligule with 1-mm scale; undamaged terminal comb tip showing whether last unit is rudimentary spikelet or naked rachis; intact ~5–6 mm spikelet and separated two glumes, fertile lemma with central/lateral awn origins, reduced sterile floret with its own three awns; same-scale B. hirsuta and B. pectinata comparison. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify five physically archived JPEGs and the remote-only public-domain seed reference separately; individual CC BY-SA 2.0, CC BY-NC and US federal public-domain provenance; Joey photo-level CC BY-NC version and noncommercial display conditions; four preexisting gross-organ arrows, six historical teaching panels, different-species label, EXIF/GPS handling and phone/mobile overlay. Do not add speculative arrows or mark FINISHED until botanical identity, rights and pixel targets are verified.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: six historical image records, five physically archived JPGs and one remote-only seed reference; critical macro and rights/site checks remain.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: LOOK HERE FIRST: typically ONE to THREE curved combs or 'eyebrows' clustered at the TOP of the flowering stem, with many closely packed spikelets all the way to the raceme tip. Blue grama normally does NOT leave a long naked pointed tip beyond the final spikelet; compare with hairy grama's stinger.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: PUBLIC PHOTO FIRST: Patrick Alexander's CC0 original photographs mature long, one-sided curved eyebrow-shaped flowering branches and their fine awnlike projections. It is actual blue grama, not a generic grass or a different species.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Follow basal shoots to a single root crown. Short stout rhizomes can occur, but a low matlike stand photograph is NOT evidence of connected rhizomes or rooting stolons. Open the INNER blade–sheath junction to find the actual short ligule ring/fringe of hairs; separate it from longer lateral collar hairs. SDSU gives <0.5 mm; Utah flora describes the entire ring <1 mm. No archived image resolves the calibrated inner ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew GrassBase gives 1–3(4) arcuate branches 1.5–5 cm long and 5–6 mm laterally compressed spikelets. Count crowded spikelets along one intact branch; the literature often reports roughly 30–90 per branch, but no archived overview permits a precise count. Pale dangling anthers are NOT glumes, lemmas or awns. Photograph an attached mature comb beside a ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Blue grama usually bears 1–3 long curved terminal eyebrow combs whose spikelets extend nearly to the end. Hairy grama often has dense long hairs and a conspicuously bare terminal rachis projection. Pectinata is generally taller with longer and often more numerous combs but overlaps hairy. Texas grama has several much shorter bristly clustered branches. Sideoats has many short side branches all the way down a long stem.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: FIELD HABIT · short blue grama foliage forming a matlike patch — archived photograph
panels.caption: Photographed in Montana, not Hays County. Short narrow basal leaves form a low, somewhat matlike patch among rocks and other vegetation; some curved combs are visible nearby. The photograph does NOT demonstrate one intact rooted plant, underground rhizomes, stolon rooting, a true ligule, or the number of combs on a single stem.

panels.label: ACTUAL MATURE BLUE GRAMA BRANCHES — fine spikelet projections on curved eyebrows (Patrick Alexander CC0)
panels.caption: Real blue grama mature flowering branches in the Organ Mountains, New Mexico. Follow the long arcuate upper comb and its hundreds of fine pale projections, then compare the narrower upright branch in front. Their curvature is useful; a single branch is not a mm-level spikelet, ligule or glume dissection.
panels.creator: Patrick Alexander
panels.modifications: No crop, GPS/EXIF stripped RGB JPEG.

markers.label: Fine awnlike projections on attached comb

panels.label: TRUE FLOWERING ANATOMY — real dangling green pollen anthers on attached blue grama comb
panels.caption: These green-yellow dangling structures are pollen-bearing anthers of actual flowering blue grama, not awns! Follow the central one-sided comb and see that long anthers project downward from many spikelets. The many stiff slender bristles are surrounding spikelet structures; their individual origins require a detached, measured spikelet.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: Resized original preserving uncropped source composition; recompressed GPS/EXIF-free; two non-destructive in-gallery arrows only.

memory_rule: Count the conspicuous curved eyebrows on ONE flowering stem, avoiding nearby stems behind the subject.
safety_note: 10 original blue grama photo records (7 public-eligible, 3 NC research holds), true hanging anthers and 2016 Smithsonian pressed fibrous roots installed. Root specimen is preserved, not living! Exact free inner 0.1–0.4 mm ciliate ligule still UNPHOTOGRAPHED; individual fertile lemma and glumes have NOT been dissected in a verified scaled photo. Public Pages and mobile arrow QA pending.
